TOPICS: bilateral relations, public opinion, defense spending, military force, foreign policy partners, international cooperation, economic power, favorable opinions, age differences, partisan divides, ideological differences, regional divides

TEXT_EVIDENCE:
- Americans' positive view of U.S.-Germany relations increased to 75% in 2019, up 7 percentage points from 2017 (Page 4)
- Only 34% of Germans say the relationship is good, with 2% saying it is very good (Page 4)
- Young people in both countries are more optimistic about the relationship (Page 4)
- Young people in both the U.S. and Germany have more positive views of the U.S.-German relationship compared to older adults (Page 5)
- In the U.S., 82% of people ages 18 to 29 say the relationship is good, compared with 73% of those ages 65 and older (Page 5)
- In Germany, four-in-ten young people (40%) say relations with the U.S. are good, compared with only 31% of those 65 and older (Page 5)
- Six-in-ten Americans (60%) say their country should defend a NATO ally against a Russian attack (Page 6)
- An equal share of Germans (60%) say their country should not (Page 6)
- 63% of Germans believe the U.S. would defend a NATO ally in a conflict with Russia (Page 6)
- About eight-in-ten Americans (78%) believe military force is sometimes necessary to maintain world order (Page 6)
- Only about half of Germans (47%) agree (Page 6)
- In the U.S., 90% of conservatives see military force as necessary, while 65% of liberals agree (Page 6)
- In Germany, nearly six-in-ten adults on the right see military force as necessary, while about a third on the left agree (Page 6)
- Half of Americans (50%) say European allies should keep defense spending the same in 2019 (Page 7)
- In 2017, 45% of Americans believed European allies should increase spending (Page 7)
- In 2019, 40% of Germans want to increase defense spending, while 41% want to keep it the same (Page 7)
- In 2017, 32% of Germans wanted to increase spending, while 51% were content with current levels (Page 7)
- Relatively few in both countries believe Europeans are spending too much on national defense, and this share has been stable since 2017 (Page 7)
- Republican support for increased defense spending from Europe fell by 14 percentage points between 2017 and 2019 (Page 8)
- In the U.S., Republicans and Republican-leaning independents are more likely than Democrats to favor increased defense spending in Europe (Page 8)
- In Germany, 51% of CDU/CSU supporters want to increase defense spending, 41% of SPD supporters, and 28% of Greens supporters (Page 8)
- 85% of Americans believe U.S. military bases in Germany are important to U.S. security (Page 9)
- 56% of Americans consider them "very important" (Page 9)
- 45% of Germans disagree that the bases are important for German security (Page 9)
- Among Republicans and Republican-leaning independents, 90% see the bases as important (Page 9)
- Among Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents, 80% see the bases as important (Page 9)
- 62% of Germans aged 18-29 think U.S. military bases do not contribute to German national security (Page 10)
- 61% of Germans aged 65 and older believe the bases are important to Germany's defense (Page 10)
- Among Americans, 36% choose the United Kingdom as the most or second-most important foreign policy partner (Page 11)
- 23% of Americans name China and 20% name Canada as top partners (Page 11)
- Only 13% of Americans see Germany as a top partner, compared to 15% for Israel and 12% for Mexico (Page 11)
- Among Germans, 60% name France as the most or second-most important partner (Page 11)
- 42% of Germans name the U.S. as a top partner, up from 35% in 2018 (Page 11)
- In the U.S., Republicans and Republican-leaning independents are keener on Israel (26%) as a foreign policy partner than Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents (9%) (Page 12)
- Both Republicans and Democrats agree that the UK is their most important partner (Page 12)
- Democrats place more emphasis on Canada (23%) and Mexico (15%) for their top foreign policy affiliate (Page 12)
- Views of Germany are similar among U.S. partisans, with both sides ranking it fifth (Page 12)
- Nearly seven-in-ten Americans (69%) say they want to cooperate more with Germany, compared with only half of Germans (50%) (Page 12)
- The percentage of Germans who want to cooperate more with the U.S. has increased nine points since 2018, when 47% wanted to cooperate less (Page 12)
- Americans are more likely than Germans to want more cooperation with the UK (76% vs. 51%) (Page 13)
- A greater share of Germans want to cooperate more with Russia (66%) than Americans (35%) (Page 13)
- Increased cooperation with Russia is more common among Republicans in the U.S. (41%) than Democrats (32%) (Page 13)
- Germans living in former East Germany (75%) are more likely to want cooperation with Russia than those in the former West (63%) (Page 13)
- Democrats in the U.S. are more likely to want greater cooperation with Germany than Republicans (75% vs. 63%) (Page 14)
- In Germany, supporters of CDU/CSU are more willing to want greater cooperation with the U.S. than those who support the Greens (45%) and the SPD (47%) (Page 14)
- When asked to choose between having a close relationship to Germany or Russia, Americans clearly favor Germany (61% to 26%) (Page 14)
- When Germans are asked to choose between Russia and the U.S., the gap is smaller (39% to 25%), and three-in-ten Germans volunteer both (Page 14)
- As it relates to a rising China, attitudes diverge the other way. Germans are about twice as likely to say they prefer a close relationship to the U.S. over China (50% to 24%), while Americans are almost equally divided (41% prefer Germany, 44% say China) (Page 14)
- 58% of Americans ages 18-29 say it is more important for their country to have a close relationship with China than with Germany (Page 15)
- 32% of Americans ages 18-29 say it is more important to have a close relationship with Germany (Page 15)
- Among older Americans, more say the relationship with Germany is more important than with China (Page 15)
- 66% of Democrats prefer close ties with Germany, compared to 57% of Republicans (Page 15)
- 31% of Republicans prefer close relations with Russia, compared to 21% of Democrats (Page 15)
- Nearly four-in-ten East Germans (38%) say they prefer close ties with Russia, compared with only 23% who say the same about the U.S. (Page 15)
- West Germans are twice as likely to prefer a close relationship with the U.S. than with Russia (Page 15)
- Half of Americans (50%) name the U.S. as the world's leading economic power (Page 16)
- About a third of Americans (32%) choose China (Page 16)
- Roughly half of Germans (53%) name China as the leading economic power (Page 16)
- 24% of Germans name the U.S. as the leading economic power (Page 16)
- 14% of Germans name the EU, which is about twice as many as in the U.S. (6%) (Page 16)
- Germans tend to view international organizations and countries more positively than Americans (Page 17)
- Roughly seven-in-ten Germans favor the EU, compared to only about half of Americans (Page 17)
- There is a wide gap between German and American perceptions of Russia, with 37% of Germans having a favorable view versus 18% of Americans (Page 17)
- About one-in-five Americans express no opinion of either the EU or NATO (Page 17)
- Conservative Americans and Germans are more likely to view Russia favorably, while liberals favor the UN and EU (Page 18)
- Ideological divides are notably wider between Americans than between Germans (Page 18)
- 43% of Germans in former East Germany have a favorable opinion of Russia, compared to 31% in the former West (Page 18)
- 71% of Germans in the former West favor the EU, compared to 59% in the former East (Page 18)

- An equal share of Germans (60%) say their country should not (Page 6)

- Only about half of Germans (47%) agree (Page 6)
- In the U.S., 90% of conservatives see military force as necessary, while 65% of liberals agree (Page 6)
- In Germany, nearly six-in-ten adults on the right see military force as necessary, while about a third on the left agree (Page 6)
- Half of Americans (50%) say European allies should keep defense spending the same in 2019 (Page 7)
- In 2017, 45% of Americans believed European allies should increase spending (Page 7)
- In 2019, 40% of Germans want to increase defense spending, while 41% want to keep it the same (Page 7)
- In 2017, 32% of Germans wanted to increase spending, while 51% were content with current levels (Page 7)
- Relatively few in both countries believe Europeans are spending too much on national defense, and this share has been stable since 2017 (Page 7)
- Republican support for increased defense spending from Europe fell by 14 percentage points between 2017 and 2019 (Page 8)
- In the U.S., Republicans and Republican-leaning independents are more likely than Democrats to favor increased defense spending in Europe (Page 8)
- In Germany, 51% of CDU/CSU supporters want to increase defense spending, 41% of SPD supporters, and 28% of Greens supporters (Page 8)
- 85% of Americans believe U.S. military bases in Germany are important to U.S. security (Page 9)
- 56% of Americans consider them "very important" (Page 9)
- 45% of Germans disagree that the bases are important for German security (Page 9)
- Among Republicans and Republican-leaning independents, 90% see the bases as important (Page 9)
- Among Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents, 80% see the bases as important (Page 9)
- 62% of Germans aged 18-29 think U.S. military bases do not contribute to German national security (Page 10)
- 61% of Germans aged 65 and older believe the bases are important to Germany's defense (Page 10)
- Among Americans, 36% choose the United Kingdom as the most or second-most important foreign policy partner (Page 11)
- 23% of Americans name China and 20% name Canada as top partners (Page 11)
- Only 13% of Americans see Germany as a top partner, compared to 15% for Israel and 12% for Mexico (Page 11)
- Among Germans, 60% name France as the most or second-most important partner (Page 11)
- 42% of Germans name the U.S. as a top partner, up from 35% in 2018 (Page 11)
- In the U.S., Republicans and Republican-leaning independents are keener on Israel (26%) as a foreign policy partner than Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents (9%) (Page 12)
- Both Republicans and Democrats agree that the UK is their most important partner (Page 12)
- Democrats place more emphasis on Canada (23%) and Mexico (15%) for their top foreign policy affiliate (Page 12)
- Views of Germany are similar among U.S. partisans, with both sides ranking it fifth (Page 12)
- Nearly seven-in-ten Americans (69%) say they want to cooperate more with Germany, compared with only half of Germans (50%) (Page 12)
- The percentage of Germans who want to cooperate more with the U.S. has increased nine points since 2018, when 47% wanted to cooperate less (Page 12)
- Americans are more likely than Germans to want more cooperation with the UK (76% vs. 51%) (Page 13)
- A greater share of Germans want to cooperate more with Russia (66%) than Americans (35%) (Page 13)
- Increased cooperation with Russia is more common among Republicans in the U.S. (41%) than Democrats (32%) (Page 13)

- Among older Americans, more say the relationship with Germany is more important than with China (Page 15)

- West Germans are twice as likely to prefer a close relationship with the U.S. than with Russia (Page 15)

elements.text: Methodology: U.S. survey

This analysis in this report is based on telephone interviews conducted September 17-22, 2019 among a national sample of 1,004 adults, 18 years of age or older, living in the United States (302 respondents were interviewed on a landline telephone, and 702 were interviewed on a cell phone, including 492 who had no landline telephone). The survey was conducted under the direction of SSRS. A combination of landline and cell phone random digit dial samples were used. Interviews were conducted in English (969) and Spanish (35). Respondents in the landline sample were selected by randomly asking for the youngest adult male or female who is now at home. Interviews in the cell sample were conducted with the person who answered the phone, if that person was an adult 18 years of age or older. For detailed information about our survey methodology, see http://www.pewresearch.org/methodology/u-s-survey-research/

The combined landline and cellphone sample are weighted to provide nationally representative estimates of the adult population 18 years of age and older. The weighting process takes into account the disproportionate probabilities of household and respondent selection due to the number of separate telephone landlines and cellphones answered by respondents and their households, as well as the probability associated with the random selection of an individual household member. Following application of the above weights, the sample is post-stratified and balanced by key demographics such as age, race, sex, region, and education. The sample is also weighted to reflect the distribution of phone usage in the general population, meaning the proportion of those who are cellphone only, landline only, and mixed users.
